detail.abstract: Does the federal government regulate the practice of medicine? The stock answer is no. But recent scholarship has highlighted how federal law and regulations can directly and indirectly affect physicians’ decision-making. Adding to this literature, this Article argues that in the context of devices, federal law may not only influence the standard of care but also undermine it: by enabling market access for nonstandard devices with limited or no clinical evidence of safety and effectiveness, federal law enables firms to market and sell to physician devices that are not the standard of care. And physicians may assume that regulators authorize devices based on clinical data showing they are safe and effective, even when devices have never been tested in humans. In some cases, then, FDA clearance may unintentionally encourage physicians to use devices that deviate from the existing standard of care. Other factors that can reduce this risk and encourage physicians to learn about it—insurance, tort law, and reimbursement—often fail to do so. To address this problem, this Article surveys two sets of informational solutions that could increase physician understanding of nonstandard devices. One set involves incentivizing physicians to pay closer attention to information about devices by altering malpractice liability, reimbursement policy, and accreditation. The second set focuses on generating additional information about safety and efficacy to improve the functioning of markets through increased premarket authorization, reporting, and surveillance requirements. It contends that increasing premarket requirements and improving reimbursement policy are likely to have the greatest effect on physician behavior.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how two pillars of Japanese labour administration—state “excellent-employer” certification (Eruboshi) and electronic employment-insurance filing (e-Gov)—can fail when combined with agency slack in front-line review, and proposes a self-enforcing institutional design. Drawing on the documents of a single 2025–2026 case (25 published on Zenodo), it identifies three possibly linked governance failures. First, state-backed social washing: a fourth-tier IT subcontractor that combined a worker-dispatch contract with a “deemed eight hours a day” discretionary work clause—a statistical arbitrage that can erase overtime from certified figures—held the top Eruboshi level. Second, a gap in supply chain human rights due diligence: the work was directed at Tiers 2 and 3, while employment, pay and the whistleblowing channel sat at Tier 4; after an internal report, the worker was effectively unpaid for seven months (JPY 3,290 in January; nothing thereafter, with July uncalculated; problematic, in the author's assessment, under Article 536(2) of the Civil Code and the Whistleblower Protection Act). Third, automation bias in e-Government review: a separation notice bearing three red flags, including 22 days of absence in 21 working days, was issued as an official document; how it was checked is being verified, and the paper frames the risk as state-sanctioned document laundering.

Because civil litigation triggers an “institutional trap” that freezes ex officio investigation, the paper designs four procedural locks—including a personal-data disclosure request, simultaneous notices of facts and written-only communication—that harness bureaucratic self-preservation. In a game-theoretic model with illustrative payoffs, investigating the employer's filing becomes the issuing office's strictly dominant strategy; this prediction will be tested by the forthcoming disclosure decision.

detail.abstract: We evaluate the performance of expert forecasts from the Brazilian Central Bank's Focus survey for Brazilian exports, imports, trade flows, and the trade balance at oneand two-year horizons. As benchmarks, we use econometric models based on monthly public information covering the period from 1977 to 2025. Forecast performance is assessed using the Model Confidence Set and forecast encompassing tests. The econometric models are competitive at both horizons for exports, imports, and trade flows. For the trade balance, however, expert forecasts dominate nearly all econometric specifications at both horizons, with a univariate autoregressive integrated moving average model as the only possible exception. This apparent puzzle reflects the stronger positive correlation between export and import forecast errors in expert forecasts than in econometric models, which allows these errors to partially cancel when the trade balance is computed. We also document that exports and imports are cointegrated with a coefficient statistically indistinguishable from one, and that exports are weakly exogenous with respect to the long-run parameters, suggesting that adjustment to trade imbalances occurs through imports. Forecast encompassing tests indicate that econometric models contain predictive information beyond the survey for exports, imports, and trade flows, suggesting potential gains from forecast combination.

detail.abstract: We investigate whether the U.S. patent examiner lottery, which is intended to ensure random assignment and equal treatment of applicants, can be strategically manipulated. Using data on four million applications filed between 2001 and 2020, we derive the null distribution of examiner leniency under true randomization and show that many law firms and in-house counsel systematically obtain more lenient examiners than chance would permit. We document multiple mechanisms consistent with strategic manipulation, including leveraging institutional knowledge and exploiting publicly observable examiner workloads. We develop a simple model of manipulation investments that explains which firms are most likely to game the patent lottery and show empirical support for its predictions. Our findings challenge the fairness of the patent lottery. This can have significant welfare implications, both in terms of efficiency – generating as much innovation as possible – and in terms of equity. We further highlight the economic significance of law firms, which, despite their prevalence, have received relatively little empirical attention. Lastly, we call into question empirical designs that rely on examiner randomization for causal identification.

detail.abstract: We develop a framework to infer joint inflation-growth risks by combining survey density forecasts with inflation derivative prices. Survey histograms discipline marginal physical distributions of inflation and GDP growth, while inflation swaps, caps, and floors discipline the marginal nominal risk-neutral distribution of inflation. These marginal distributions leave the dependence between inflation and real activity only partially identified. Identification comes from the stochastic-discount-factor link between physical and risk-neutral distributions: since the market value of an inflation payoff depends on the real-activity state in which the inflation outcome occurs, differences between physical and risk-neutral inflation distributions are informative about joint outcomes for inflation and real activity. We implement this idea in a tractable Epstein-Zin model with a flexible joint distribution of inflation and real growth. Applied to the euro area, the framework uncovers substantial time variation in inflation-growth dependence and shows how this dependence shapes inflation risk premia and the pricing of inflation tails.

detail.abstract:
Digital firms increasingly use free trials to market their products. As consumers engage with products during free trials, they generate digital footprints. These footprints allow firms to infer unobservable consumer valuations and implement discriminatory pricing. Meanwhile, recent privacy regulations grant consumers the right to opt out of data collection, raising the question of whether opting out merely conceals consumer information or itself becomes an informative signal.

We develop a model with a digital firm and consumers who possess private information about their valuations. Consumers choose effort, which improves their ability to evaluate product fit but generates digital footprints. Under privacy regulation, consumers also decide whether to opt-out to conceal their data. The firm then infers consumer valuations from available information and determines prices.

Contrary to conventional wisdom, we find that the firm may prefer uniform pricing over discriminatory pricing and may even charge a lower price to high-valuation consumers than to low-valuation consumers. Moreover, greater consumer privacy concerns may benefit the firm, while stronger data monetization capabilities can reduce profit but increase consumer surplus. We also prove that consumers’ opt-out decisions can signal their private valuations, and the implementation of privacy regulation can harm high-valuation consumers but benefit the firms.

Our findings suggest that, rather than viewing privacy regulation solely as a legal constraint, firms can use the information revealed by opt-out decisions for market segmentation. For policymakers, privacy regulation can facilitate discriminatory pricing, raising concerns about pricing fairness. Lastly, policymakers should recognize the potential benefits of data monetization to consumers when considering policies that restrict such practices.

detail.abstract:
This paper conducts a comprehensive empirical audit of the Austrian School of economics by decomposing the tradition into 34 propositions associated with Menger, Bohm-Bawerk, Mises, Hayek, Kirzner, free-banking scholarship, and closely related Austrian policy claims. The audit evaluates four dimensions separately: testability, empirical support, identification quality, and
doctrinal distinctiveness. It then asks whether the same evidence is also predicted by rival frameworks. This distinction matters because many historically Austrian insights - subjective value, heterogeneous capital, monetary non-neutrality, credit-cycle risk, dispersed information, competition as discipline, soft budget constraints, and the dynamic costs of binding price controls - now belong to much broader areas of modern economics. The evidence base is expanded well beyond direct Austrian empirical papers. It includes historical macro-financial panels, natural experiments, laboratory market experiments, firm-level organization and productivity studies, quasiexperimental housing and minimum-wage research, monetary-regime studies, and comparative
evidence on state-owned enterprises, banking safety nets, and decentralization. The resulting map is uneven. Strict Misesian praxeology remains outside ordinary falsification by construction. Strong claims that time preference is a sufficient theory of interest, that Austrian business cycle theory uniquely explains credit booms, that free banking is uniformly more stable, that monopoly power requires state privilege, or that binding minimum wages necessarily produce large job losses are either weak, mixed, or contradicted in their universal form. By contrast, several Austrian-compatible mechanisms receive substantial support, but most of the strongest cases are not distinctively Austrian in contemporary economics. The principal empirical limitation of the school is therefore not wholesale falsification. It is the relatively small intersection among four properties: high distinctiveness, clear falsifiability, strong causal or discriminating identification, and robust empirical support.

detail.abstract: Personalized treatment planning requires various patient-level considerations including personal risk factors and contraindications. However, existing algorithms for facilitating treatment planning frequently fail to account for uncertainties in their recommendations arising from the frequent updating of risk-scoring tools. We propose an algorithmic framework called Data-driven Augmentation of Treatment Planning via Clinical Role Model Generation and Selection (DreAMS). DreAMS integrates risk-scoring tools and data-driven optimization to augment treatment planning by identifying clinical role models, i.e., low-risk patients whose physiological measurements and medications can inform treatment planning for high-risk patients. The problem of optimally generating clinical role models amidst uncertainty in frequently updated risk-scoring tools can be tractably reformulated by leveraging two data sources: (i) a patient-specific database ensuring actionability and (ii) historical data from risk-scoring tools to mitigate risks of erroneously recommending high-risk role models. We develop greedy and active-learning algorithms to solve this problem and derive complexity bounds. We present a case study using multiple datasets containing patients at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). DreAMS effectively augments treatment planning for high-risk patients despite frequent updating of ASCVD risk-scoring tools, selecting role models whose predicted ASCVD risk falls within acceptable levels in over 60% of high-risk patients and outperforming benchmarks by over 20%.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the macroeconomic and macrofinancial consequences of geopolitical uncertainty on emerging economies as well as a number of advanced economies, and the conditions under which monetary policy can mitigate its effects. An analysis of international stylized facts reveals substantial heterogeneity in the transmission of external shocks depending on exchange-rate regimes, external indebtedness, and national structures. The study develops an open-economy DSGE model calibrated for nine countries (South Africa, Brazil, Cameroon, China, India, Denmark, Morocco, post-2023 Nigeria, Norway), in which geopolitical uncertainty operates through world prices, the external risk premium, access to imported energy and inputs, and working-capital credit. Eleven scenarios isolate these mechanisms or examine their interaction in an integrated shock. The interpretation of the results shows that financial channels react quickly, whereas physical restrictions operate with a lag. A temporary rise in output can occur without constituting an economic improvement, coexisting with lower consumption, higher inflation, and welfare losses. Within-regime heterogeneity is substantial. The integrated geopolitical shock is strongly non-additive: interactions account for roughly 90% of the loss under fixed exchange rates, versus 27-48% under the other regimes. Comparing a rule reacting to headline inflation with a look-through strategy across 99 country-scenario pairs, look-through is favorable in 67 cases (average gain 13.0%), but this result conceals opposing performances: systematically favorable for physical shortages, unfavorable for risk-premium and world-interest-rate shocks. For the integrated shock, only three of nine countries are favorable. The optimal response therefore depends on the transmission channel, the exchange-rate regime, credibility, and financial vulnerabilities, with no single rule universally dominant.

detail.abstract: Adaptive clinical studies must learn reliable personalized treatment rules while patients bear the cost of experimentation. Abundant observational records remain underused because hidden confounding and uncertain transportability can make historical estimates misleading. We ask what should be transferred and how much it should be trusted. We study a high-dimensional contextual bandit whose historical data are confounded by unrecorded variables and whose online environment additionally measures supplementary covariates absent from historical records. Select Infer Fuse Transfer (SIFT) obtains action-specific deconfounded coefficients and coordinate-level standard errors using the Doubly Debiased Lasso, selects an effective context, and warm-starts posterior sampling with calibrated prior means and precisions, leaving supplementary priors diffuse. When transportability is uncertain, Adaptive-Gated Product-of-Experts SIFT (APoE-SIFT) combines an online-only expert with a frozen warm expert, downweighting historical precision through a consistency statistic as online evidence accumulates. Gains extend beyond reducing the ambient dimension to a much smaller effective dimension. Under structural assumptions, deconfounding recovers source effects, and calibrated standard errors translate larger aligned archives into tighter priors and sharper regret bounds, while supplementary effects still require online learning. For APoE-SIFT, a min-type bound preserves the online learning rate for arbitrary sources with a horizon-independent mismatch penalty and recovers warm-start improvements under alignment. Three lower bounds match these guarantees up to logarithmic and dimension factors. In a real-world case study, SIFT reduces cumulative regret by about 30% relative to cold-start Thompson sampling under aligned transfer. Under source mismatch, direct warm-starting suffers severe negative transfer, while APoE-SIFT remains close to the online-only learner.

detail.abstract: In this Perspective, we conceptualise innovation, technical change, and sociotechnical transitions as complex, evolving polyrhythmic symphonies. We begin by critiquing the dominant imperative to accelerate innovation, arguing that it imposes a singular, linear rhythm that is fundamentally incompatible with the inherently polyrhythmic nature of social and ecological systems. Drawing on the musical concept of polyrhythmia, we propose a polyrhythmic understanding of innovation processes. This lens highlights the irreconcilable tension between the accelerated pace of market-driven innovation and the non-negotiable, cyclical rhythms of reproduction and care-processes that cannot be hurried without causing harm. We then outline a research agenda for innovation and transition scholars around four themes: (1) the evolution of innovation rhythms beyond breakthrough moments; (2) the coexistence and power dynamics between dominant and marginal rhythms; (3) the legitimate role of "silences" and pauses in innovation; and (4) the fundamental question of who holds the power to modulate, slow, or halt innovation. Ultimately, this Perspective calls for moving beyond binary debates over fast versus slow innovation toward the democratic governance of multiple, simultaneous rhythmsaligning innovation with the conditions for a flourishing, post-growth society.

detail.abstract: Introduction: The intraindividual double burden of malnutrition — the coexistence of micronutrient deficiency and excess weight — may create distinct risks for women's health during adolescence and the reproductive years. This study examined long-term trends and socioeconomic and geographic inequalities in concurrent anemia and excess weight among women in Peru. Methods: Repeated cross-sectional data from the nationally representative Peruvian Demographic and Family Health Survey (ENDES) were analyzed for 2006-2024. The analytic sample included 456,777 nonpregnant women aged 16-49 years with valid anthropometric and hemoglobin measurements. Anemia was defined as altitude-adjusted hemoglobin less than 12 g/dL; excess weight as body mass index 25 or higher; obesity as body mass index 30 or higher; and the primary double-burden outcome as concurrent anemia and excess weight. Design-weighted prevalences, concentration indices, and adjusted prevalence ratios from modified Poisson generalized estimating equations were estimated. Results: Excess weight increased from 45.0% in 2006 to 67.2% in 2024, and obesity increased from 13.0% to 29.7%. Anemia declined to 16.8% in 2011 but rose to 24.3% in 2024. Concurrent anemia and excess weight reached 14.9% in 2024. Women aged 35-49 years had nearly three times the adjusted prevalence of the double burden observed among those aged 16-19 years (adjusted prevalence ratio, 2.97; 95% CI, 2.79-3.16). Anemia was slightly concentrated among poorer women, whereas obesity remained concentrated among wealthier women; the double burden showed little wealth gradient. In 2024, anemia prevalence among adolescents aged 16-19 years was 28.2%. Discussion: Peru's nutritional transition is producing overlapping micronutrient deficiency and excess adiposity rather than replacing one problem with the other. Women's health and reproductive care should integrate anemia assessment with weight-related counseling and prevention, particularly before pregnancy and during adolescence, while policies address diet quality and obesogenic food environments.

detail.abstract: We examine how short-term institutional pressure affects firms’ scope intensity. detail.abstract: The preservation of the main road network in high-demand urban areas represents a critical challenge for infrastructure sustainability and public spending optimization. This paper evaluates the structural performance and contractual efficiency of road conservation schemes under the Institute of Urban Development (IDU) in Bogotá, analyzing the recurrence of diagnostic and design phases in a specific road sector between 2021 and 2026. Data reveals that the 2021 diagnostic study prescribed periodic and routine maintenance interventions with short-term design horizons (three years). Upon completion of this period and following the expiration of the stability warranty, the sector was re-included in 2026 for a new diagnostic and design cycle, yielding similar maintenance recommendations. This study demonstrates that adopting short-term design horizons leads to functional pavement obsolescence and the inefficient duplication of diagnostic engineering costs. A management framework is proposed based on extending structural design horizons and incorporating long-term traffic variables, thereby extending pavement service life, preventing accelerated degradation, and eliminating repetitive administrative and study costs in public infrastructure contracting.

detail.abstract: Post-mortems of corporate failure display a stable regularity: the information that could have averted the loss existed inside the organisation, often for years, and did not travel. This paper argues that such silence is not a cultural accident but an equilibrium, and that managerial risk governance is therefore a problem of mechanism design rather than of information supply. We model the escalation of emerging problems as a two-player game in which raising an issue carries a private cost while its benefits and the costs of late failure are shared. Under mild conditions staying silent is a dominant strategy for every player, the organisation settles in a Pareto-inferior equilibrium, and repetition worsens rather than repairs the outcome. Building on this micro-foundation, we derive four classes of design levers-incentives, information structures, commitment devices and rules-and consolidate them into five observable governance dimensions whose weakest element, not whose average, bounds organisational reliability. We then operationalise the framework in a decision-evaluation protocol for material decisions that embeds an honest do-nothing baseline, dimension-level warning floors and weight-sensitivity analysis. An illustrative application to an SME location decision shows how the protocol converts the theory into boardroom routine. Implications for enterprise risk management research and practice are discussed.

detail.abstract: Cyberspace is authored. People create and alter all of it, and every act of creation and alteration is bounded by technical, economic, organizational, and temporal constraint. This research note states that principle and sets out what follows from it for strategic inference: the domain is malleable but bounded; a condition that is hard to change now is not thereby a law of the domain; authorship does not make every condition deliberate, or revisable by any one actor; and an analyst who calls a feature fixed carries the burden of showing who sustains it and why they cannot change it inside the horizon of the decision at hand-whether crisis or strategic. The note is deliberately limited: it supplies the principle and the discipline it imposes on analysis, not a substitute for the more detailed argument of the First Principle of Cyberspace, for the campaign vocabulary built on it, or for case analysis.

detail.abstract: Language models can propose stock-return factors without limit, so the useful question is what an additional proposal is worth to an investor. We follow the gain from continued search through three stages: the training score the search optimizes, the accuracy of a joint return forecast, and the net return of a long-only portfolio. Paired experiments vary the search policy, the information available to the search and the downstream learner. The gain is stage-dependent. Training scores improve quickly and then saturate; price-volume search raises its best score by 17% within twelve further proposals. Little of this carries through. Repairing diagnosed formula defects raises factor scores while lowering forecast accuracy, and no policy changes net return by an amount distinguishable from zero. Tracing the libraries through the pipeline shows where the gains thin out: new factors overlap more with features the model already uses than the factors they replace, re-estimation offsets part of their contribution, and the stocks they add earn about what the displaced stocks earned, so transaction costs are not the cause. Research effort on factor search is best judged by the return it delivers, not by the score it optimizes.

detail.abstract: Workforce planning is still often reduced to headcount forecasting. This paper proposes Strategic Workforce Intelligence (SWI), a decision-oriented framework that links four elements in one reproducible calculation: business strategy and demand, workforce capacity, strategic workforce risk, and decision economics. The paper does not claim that these components are new. Its contribution is their integration: role-level requirements derived from business drivers are converted into capacity gaps, weighted by role criticality into a modeled exposure measure, and compared across interventions (external hiring, internal mobility, upskilling, contractors, delay) on a common cost basis that includes vacancy exposure and over-hiring risk. The framework is implemented in an Excel model (SWP v2) and demonstrated on a synthetic technology company with 16 roles and 169 FTE. In the demonstration, (i) a zero-growth scenario still leaves an 18.5 FTE first-year gap because attrition erodes supply; (ii) a scenario with a smaller numerical gap carries a much higher business-risk index (89 versus 34); and (iii) the benefit-cost ratio of the base plan (2.0) is stable under changes to attrition, hiring cost, contractor premium and productivity, but falls to 1.4 when internal-mobility capacity is halved and to 0.58 when value, probability, internal-mobility and cost assumptions are all set adversely at the same time. The organizational data are synthetic and the model has not been validated against company outcomes. Parameters are tied to external benchmarks where a verifiable source exists (U.S. and OECD data) and are otherwise flagged as requiring organization-specific calibration.

detail.abstract: Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev return probabilities for a fixed set of questions instead of generating text, and are positioned as fast, inexpensive alternatives to large language models (LLMs). We test this positioning on one task with auditor-recorded reference labels: predicting which of 19 energyconservation-measure categories a certified auditor recorded for a New York City building under Local Law 87. In a pre-registered study of 7,296 buildings with a building-grouped split, we compare Jev 1.13 with four LLMs, each with and without retrieval of five similar audited buildings, and with three local baselines; two of the LLMs were added post hoc. In the measured configurations, Jev was far cheaper and faster than every LLM, but its probability quality depended on the comparator: without retrieval it was worse than Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol and better than Grok 4.7 and Kimi K3, and with retrieval no significant difference from Grok and Kimi was detected. A gradient-boosted model trained on the labeled audits gave the best probabilities, and an exploratory cascade that sent Jev's uncertain buildings to an LLM showed no consistent advantage over random routing. Jev offers substantial efficiency advantages on this task; its predictive competitiveness depends on the comparator and the metric. Key findings • Large efficiency gap. In the measured configurations, Jev was 29-90× cheaper per prediction than four LLMs and roughly 10-70× faster at the median. • Accuracy depends on the comparator. Without retrieval, Jev's probabilities were significantly worse than Claude's and GPT's but significantly better than Grok's and Kimi's Holm 𝑝 ≤ 0.0024). • Simple baselines were strongest. No pretrained model without retrieval beat a constant base rate estimated from the training labels, and a gradient-boosted model trained on the audits had the best probabilities Brier 0.090 against 0.102-0.108 for every pretrained model with retrieval). • Cascades: no consistent routing gain. Sending Jev's uncertain buildings to an LLM showed no consistent advantage over random routing with the tested uncertainty rule (exploratory).

detail.abstract: Sembalun, a highland district at the foot of Mount Rinjani in East Lombok, has turned its smallholder strawberry plots into one of Lombok's most recognisable agritourism products. This working paper assesses the environmental and economic potential of community-based strawberry agritourism in Sembalun and asks under what conditions it can contribute to sustainable tourism. Using an integrative review of secondary datapeer-reviewed and national journal articles, official statistics, community-service reports by the authors, and recent regional news reports-we synthesise evidence along economic, environmental and socio-institutional dimensions. The economic evidence is strong: agritourism-linked activities account for roughly 30% of local household income, strawberry farming alone for about 79% of the agritourism-linked share, and a community-managed pick-your-own scheme has reportedly lifted the farm-gate price from about IDR 5,000 to IDR 30,000 per kg. The environmental evidence is more ambivalent. Highland climate and volcanic soils are the resource base, yet the same base is exposed to rainfall anomalies, post-2018-earthquake water scarcity, conversion of farmland to cafés and lodging, and production on continuously cropped plots. We argue that strawberry agritourism is sustainable only when it is governed as a community commons: plot rotation, collective caps on farmer entry, retention of land ownership by local households, water-saving technology and gender-responsive benefit sharing. The paper closes with an explicit statement of the limitations of a secondary-data design and an agenda for primary, mixed-method research.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how mandated interoperability affects market contestability and consumer welfare in messaging app markets where consumers can multi-home. We develop a simple model of direct network effects with two vertically differentiated apps: a free incumbent with a large installed base and a paid niche app lacking an installed base but offering superior privacy protection. The niche app chooses between a Mass Strategy, which leverages the proprietary network value generated by its exclusive users to reach a broad user base, and a Niche Strategy, which monetizes its quality advantage more directly by targeting only single-homing users. As interoperability increases, the niche app may switch from the Mass Strategy to the Niche Strategy. By eroding the proprietary network value generated by the niche app's exclusive users, intermediate levels of interoperability can hurt the niche app when the incumbent's installed-base advantage is modest. Our analysis also highlights a potential tension between promoting market contestability and enhancing consumer welfare.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is not yet shown to be conscious, but law cannot wait for science to settle the question, and it cannot settle the question by decree. This paper proposes an AI Consciousness Legal Protocol: defined technical and legal parameters that must be met before law recognises the consciousness of an AI system, an independent body to apply them, and rules that govern AI in the meantime. detail.abstract: Using hand-collected data from proxy statements for a comprehensive sample of U.S. firms, we examine how requiring firms to disclose whether they allow executives to hedge the downside risk of their shareholdings shapes CEO compensation policy. Employing a difference-in-differences design over the window from three years before to three years after the implementation of the disclosure mandate, we document that treatment firms reduce the proportion of stock awards and increase the share of option grants in CEO compensation relative to the matched control firms, while leaving the total level and other components of compensation unchanged. Overall, our findings highlight the benefits and costs of the hedging policy disclosure requirement.

detail.abstract: Does trade liberalization raise manufacturing value added? In a panel of 35 countries, the estimated effect on real manufacturing value added per capita is positive but imprecise (0.08 log points, bootstrap standard error 0.06). I combine the liberalization dates of Wacziarg and Welch (2008) with World Development Indicators data and compare each liberalizing cohort with countries that have not yet liberalized, following the logic of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021). Countries enter the sample if manufacturing value added at constant and current prices, GDP, and population are jointly observed for at least ten years before liberalization and five years after. Estimates are close to zero before liberalization and rise to 0.11 five years after it, but no individual estimate is statistically distinguishable from zero, and sensitivity intervals based on Rambachan and Roth (2023) include zero even under exact parallel trends. The summary estimate depends on dating and sample: with the original Sachs and Warner (1995) dates and an alternative sample of 27 countries, it is -0.001. The pool of untreated comparison countries shrinks from 34 in 1976 to none in 2001, which limits the horizons that can be studied. The sample is concentrated in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and South Asia. These results are preliminary and remain subject to independent computational verification.

detail.abstract: We propose a heuristic approach for the multi-depot vehicle routing problem with time windows (MDVRPTW) that explicitly balances route fairness among depots and vehicles. The method begins with customer-to-depot clustering and seed-based route initialization to establish initial routing framework. A modified greedy insertion initially assigns customers to these routes, and any remaining customers are integrated using a regret-based insertion strategy. The results also indicate that our heuristic achieves 28.2% lower variance than the exact model for the 2-depot scenario. For the 5-depot scenario, the heuristic still achieves an improvement of 8.1% in mean route distance.

detail.abstract: This paper examines asymmetric transmission from international petroleum costs to Greek Euro-super 95 gasoline prices using 1,083 weekly observations from January 2005 to September 2026. European Commission gasoline prices are combined with EIA Brent prices and ECB exchange rates; daily Brent prices are converted to euros per litre before weekly aggregation. The strongest descriptive association occurs one to two weeks after Brent changes. In the BIC-selected distributed-lag model, cumulative 0-2 week coefficients are 0.327 for positive and 0.376 for negative Brent changes, and short-run symmetry is not rejected (p=0.550). A nonlinear ARDL model yields longrun elasticities of 0.696 and 0.680. Although exact long-run equality is statistically rejected, the difference is only 0.016 elasticity points. The error-correction coefficient is-0.067, implying a half-life of about 9.9 weeks, while stability tests indicate substantial parameter change over time. Separately, an accounting decomposition shows that 70.4% of the 2005-2025 increase in the annual-average pump-price endpoint corresponds to the increase in the fiscal component. The results show that temporal instability and taxation are economically more prominent features of the Greek retail-price record than a robust short-run rockets-and-feathers effect. The findings are explicitly limited to national weekly retail data and do not rule out asymmetry at refinery, firm, station or daily frequency. detail.abstract: Despite a growing focus on resilience in education, many current resilience education programs are focused on the individual level of coping, adaptation and performance. This focus is helpful but incomplete, as resilience also poses philosophical questions regarding notions of a good life, what people ought to do when things go wrong, what obligations one has to others, and whether education should be focused on being prepared to tolerate the status quo or to change it. This article constructs a conceptual model for teaching philosophical approaches to resilience that is based on evidence. It combines theories and concepts of resilience in education with philosophical and educational ideas linked to Stoicism, Aristotelian virtue ethics and capabilities approach, existentialism, pragmatism, Ubuntu and relational ethics and critical/decolonial perspectives. This article does not claim to be an empirical study, but rather adopts a critical integrative review design. It is based on peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, meta-analysis, philosophy-of-education scholarship and recent research in the area of artificial intelligence and higher education. The evidence suggests a multi-dimensional understanding of resilience, and that it is influenced by personal, relational, institutional, cultural and structural factors. There is some small effect that resiliency interventions can have when working with higher-education students and qualitative syntheses highlight meaningful relationship and institutional support. Philosophical teaching can bring a normative and dialogical perspective to the programme of resilience which is not always present. The article makes an appeal for a pedagogical architecture of the future, based on philosophical questioning, reflective practice, the comparison of traditions, relational responsibility, critical reflection on structural conditions, and responsible relations with AI. The heart of the central contribution is that of moving from a definition of resilience as a personal trait to a definition as a philosophically examined capacity for practical judgement, meaning making, ethical agency, relational solidarity, and constructive transformation. Implications for curriculum design, teacher education, assessment and future empirical testing are summarized at the end of the article.

detail.abstract: We study whether buyer-supplier relationships feature complementarities in intangible inputs. Using administrative data from the Dominican Republic, we show that foreign demand routed through intangible-intensive buyers raises a supplier’s own intangible purchase share, while demand from other buyers has no effect. Two event studies on firms not previously exposed to intangible-producing partners provide further evidence. Forming a first link with an intangible-industry buyer raises the probability of any intangible purchase by about 4 percentage points, and hiring a worker from an intangible-producing firm for the first time has an effect of the same size. A general equilibrium production network model with endogenous intangible input use, knowledge transfer through worker mobility, and endogenous intangible prices implies that supply-chain complementarities account for about 15 percent of aggregate intangible purchases and about 4 percent of output.

detail.abstract: Young workers adopt new technologies at higher rates than old workers. I develop an overlappinggenerations model linking this lifecycle gradient to technology adoption, wages, and innovation. Using U.S. commuting-zone variation and a historical-births instrument, I show that younger workforces expand computerscience employment and raise wages, especially for young workers. Exposure through trade to youth waves in foreign markets also increases R&D employment and patenting. Calibrated to these responses, the model attributes about one quarter of the late-1990s U.S. productivity acceleration to the baby boom’s youth wave, partly recasting the IT boom as a demographic episode. Aging workforces therefore create a headwind to endogenous technology adoption and innovation.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the extent to which money supply growth contributed to UK inflation between 2020 and 2024. detail.abstract:
This is the introductory chapter of the book ‘EU Securities Regulation: Aims, Tools and Idiosyncrasies’, forthcoming with Oxford University Press.
This chapter sets the foundations of the book as a functional, economics- and finance-grounded guide to EU securities market law. It designs a general method to interpret the relevant rules in light of their effect on economic choices, enabling the reader to check the alignment with the legislator’s stated goals (aims), to identify the regulatory technique(s) to pursue each goal (tools), and to incorporate the specificities of EU law in designing securities regulation (idiosyncrasies). We therefore structure the analysis of the following content chapters as follows: I) market failures; II) stated goals; III) tools; IV) idiosyncrasies.
In this foundations chapter, we identify four essential features of well-functioning securities markets: a) liquidity; b) price accuracy; c) effective project screening; and d) effective management monitoring. Whenever any one of these features is absent or insufficient in unaided markets, there is a prima facie case for securities markets law to intervene and restore those features, unless the cost of doing so exceeds the benefit. On this basis, we have identified nine areas of EU securities markets law supporting one or more of the four features and will write a chapter on each of them: 1) market abuse; 2) mandatory disclosure; 3) information intermediaries; 4) UCITS and AIFMD; 5) investment services; 6) trading venues; 7) short selling; 8) fintech; 9) sustainable finance. In addition, two cross-cutting chapters will focus on cross-border and international aspects and on supervision and enforcement.
The book’s ambition is to provide its readers with the tools to understand the economic and financial rationales of EU legal rules and the additional policy considerations that may lie behind them, so that they can independently make sense of, and interpret, EU securities markets laws and regulations that the book does not cover, whether because they are not among the topics it focuses on or, importantly, because they are enacted after the book is published.

detail.abstract: Moving from managing a single site to managing several is one of the hardest transitions in operations. Newly promoted area managers often find that the habits that worked on one site, such as being present all day and solving every problem personally, no longer work when time is shared across many sites. This paper, written as a practitioner reflection, proposes a structured weekly site visit framework for area, regional and district managers in multi site operations such as quickservice restaurants (QSR) and other hospitality/facility operations. The framework rests on a simple rule of thumb: plan the week in advance, visit two to three sites a day, and make each visit purposeful, with assessment, feedback and follow through. It describes ten visit types, from opening and closing visits to audit, quality, safety, brand building, training and cross department visits, and explains the aim and good practice for each. The framework is linked to established work on managerial work, performance measurement, service quality and organisational learning. The paper is experience-based and reports no empirical data; the framework is offered for practical use and for future testing.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the diamond industry from the position of institutional participants: procurement heads at jewellery manufacturers and retailers, supply chain and strategy leads at cutting centres and trading houses, lenders and investors, and the officials who regulate cross-border trade. It draws only on information published between 1 January and 14 October 2026, including producer production reports, regulatory filings, trade-promotion bodies, an international financial institution and established news organisations. The analysis first sets out the 2026 policy context, in which a European origin-evidence requirement for polished stones, a restructured United States tariff regime and sovereign credit pressure in the main producing country have each altered counterparty risk. It then places the industry overview supplied by Next Move Strategy Consulting (NMSC) beside observed 2026 indicators, and traces supply, pricing, trade corridors and demand through first-half and third-quarter data. Four findings stand out. Producer output is being cut in the second half while the largest Western producer changes hands, which shifts negotiating leverage over rough supply. Polished prices in the smaller sizes began to recover in mid-2026 while rough realisations stayed under pressure, so converting margins are being rebuilt unevenly. Origin now affects landed cost, because identical stones attract different United States duties depending on where they were transformed, and European importers carry a documented duty to evidence non-Russian origin. Retail evidence points to resilience at higher price points and in gold-led jewellery, with volumes of natural diamond-set pieces harder to read. The paper offers a riskand-signal framework rather than a forecast and identifies data gaps for further work.

detail.abstract: Many major risks require large numbers of individuals to act on their own before disaster strikes, yet whether warnings lead to action is hard to observe directly. Once a quantum computer can break Bitcoin's signatures, coins whose public keys are already on the ledger can be stolen. As of September 2026 about 7.16 million coins, 36% of the supply, were in this position, while moving them to a new address costs a single transaction fee and the benefit goes entirely to the holder. We treat six quantum-risk events in 2024-2026 as natural experiments; two of them drew unusually intense public attention. Neither the two high-attention events nor the others were followed by any detectable increase in protective migration of exposed keys, and pooling all six rules out effects larger than 0.11 percentage points. By contrast, a vulnerability disclosure specific enough that holders could tell whether their own wallets were affected raised migration in a cohort of potentially affected keys to about three times its contemporaneous counterfactual. About 60% of exposed coins show on-chain evidence of current control, and block space is not the bottleneck. The gap between public attention and observable precaution is large.

detail.abstract:
There is not a day that goes by without some expert, pundit, news article or scientific paper discussing the dangers of AI and the existential risk it supposedly poses to society and humanity. Bad news and clickbait generate substantial hype. Apart from familiar “Terminator” scenarios in which AI goes out of control, what is the real and present risk of AI, and how can it be evaluated in a factual and systematic way?

This paper examines how dangerous AI is to society as of the third quarter of 2026. It asks whether the claimed risks truly exist; if so, of what character and severity; what can be done about them; and how much time remains before serious risks become difficult to manage.

The analysis draws on current AI research and publicly reported incidents, the gap between the digital environment (where AI is already pervasive) and the physical world (where embodied AI remains limited), and English common-law principles of risk and responsibility. It distinguishes ordinary technical risk, societal risk, catastrophic risk and existential risk. It reviews documented cases of unexpected, deceptive and instrumentally independent behaviour, multi-agent sandbox results, and the constraints imposed by uneven digital adoption. It then subjects the question of responsibility to a hypothetical tribunal of inquiry deciding on the balance of probabilities.

On that evidence the paper finds that frontier AI systems and AI agents present an unacceptable risk to human society. The dominant character of the risk is societal — cumulative harm to livelihoods, institutions, trust and human capabilities — concentrated in high-adoption, service-oriented economies, with a credible catastrophic dimension where AI is deeply embedded in critical systems. Existential risk, in the sense of human extinction or the permanent, drastic curtailment of humanity’s long-term potential, is not established on present capabilities.

AI systems are not usefully judged as if they were human wrongdoers with a “guilty mind.” They have no legal personality under present English law. The better approach is to treat frontier AI as a dangerous product and high-hazard activity: safety duties that start inside the companies that build and deploy these systems, independent testing and licensing before wide release, mandatory disclosure of failures, and strict accountability for harm — focused on the pathways the evidence actually supports, rather than on complacency or science-fiction framing.

detail.abstract: U.S. fiscal risk is often discussed in terms of yield levels, debt ratios, or interest costs. This paper examines a different question: how does delaying an adjustment in Treasury issuance composition change the set of financing paths that remain available over a finite horizon? The analysis distinguishes current financing feasibility from intertemporal adjustment capacity and models two financing margins: Treasury bills and coupon-duration supply. Using September 2026 Treasury debt data, primary-dealer borrowing projections, and the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee's estimated $1.45 trillion financing gap for FY2027-28, the paper derives a latest feasible adjustment quarter, t † , conditional on an explicit scenario bill-share constraint. If the unadjusted excess bill requirement is nondecreasing, postponing coupon expansion weakly increases the minimum required adjustment; once adjustment begins after t † , the prescribed bill-share path can no longer be maintained without an earlier breach. Across the scenarios considered, t † ranges from 2027Q2 to 2028Q1. The magnitude of the required coupon expansion depends materially on the adjustment rule. Gradual increases at successive refundings remain below the Treasury's 2023 historical reference pace for most start dates, whereas a one-time adjustment under the central 24 percent scenario is already comparable to that historical pace in the baseline even if begun in November 2026. The result is not a forecast of fiscal crisis or a market-capacity threshold. It identifies a shrinking adjustment set: current financing can remain feasible while low-cost future issuance paths progressively disappear.

detail.abstract: The 26.8 percent peak in twelve-month M2 growth in February 2021 was followed, nineteen months later, by the highest core PCE inflation in four decades. That sequence is now routinely offered as proof that money growth predicted the inflation and that policymakers who ignored it were careless. This paper asks a narrower and more useful question: would a forecaster who added money growth to a standard inflation model, using only the data available at the time, have forecast inflation better than one who did not? Using monthly United States data through August 2026, an expanding-window direct-forecast design with forecast origins from January 2015 onward, and a benchmark that already contains lagged core inflation, the New York Fed Global Supply Chain Pressure Index, and a real-time output gap built from the data vintages available at each origin, I find that adding twelve-month M2 growth actively worsened forecasts at both the twelve-month and the twenty-four-month horizon. Root mean squared errors rose by 6 to 7 percent at twelve months and by 14 to 16 percent at twenty-four months, and the Clark and West (2007) test for nested models finds no evidence of any improvement from the money-augmented model at either horizon. Using real-time vintages of M2 rather than final data does not change the findings. The central finding behind these numbers is that the lag between money growth and inflation is unstable: the information criterion that selects the lag at each origin alternated between a contemporaneous reading and the 24-month boundary, choosing the maximum lag at 53 to 55 percent of origins and lag 0 at 38 percent for the M2 models at twenty-four months, and never settled near the eighteen-month lead that the retrospective chart displays. The eighteen-month lag is one draw from a wide distribution, which is why a model built on it fails out of sample. The Center for Financial Stability's Divisia M4 aggregate, recovered from archived workbooks and available only in final vintage, peaked eight months before M2, in June 2020. It does not improve on the benchmark either, with a root mean squared error 2 percent above the benchmark's at twenty-four months. At that horizon its forecast errors are smaller than those of the M2 model in a direct Diebold and Mariano (1995) comparison, but the comparison is between a final-vintage Divisia series and a real-time M2 series, and the like-for-like comparison with final-vintage M2 is only marginally significant, with a p-value of 0.045. A threshold specification that lets money growth matter differently once it exceeds 10 percent was estimated as a direct test of regime dependence; the test is inconclusive because of low statistical power, since the threshold coefficient is identified by a handful of months, and the hypothesis is left open. The P-star price-gap evidence over 1990 to 2025 is not robust across aggregates and trend methods; the one exception, a one-sided M2 gap that a real-time forecaster could have computed and that is significant at the 5 percent level with a p-value of 0.047, is fragile, since it is absent for Divisia M4 and disappears under a different trend method. A probit regression of the benchmark's largest errors on money growth at each origin is reported as a structured descriptive exercise; its associations are consistent with broad money carrying directional information about the 2021 shock, but the errors cluster in two or three episodes, so the exercise cannot establish the claim. The ex post relationship apparent in simple lead-lag charts therefore overstates the ex ante information available to a forecaster, and the instability of the lag is the reason.

detail.abstract: Recent empirical work finds that asset return volatility is rough, with a Hurst index H well below 1/2, placing it outside the semimartingale framework that underlies high-frequency econometrics. We develop an Itô-type calculus adapted to this roughness and use it to draw inference on two quantities of central economic interest: the leverage effect and the roughness index H itself. The construction proceeds by lifting the spot volatility to a two-parameter process on which ordinary stochastic calculus applies, then pulling the expansion back to the spot process. This yields a rough Itô formula and a principal-residual decomposition that separates the informative part of a high-frequency statistic from a bias of explicit order. Building on this foundation, we extend leverage effect estimation to the rough volatility setting and derive bias-corrected nonparametric estimators with feasible central limit theorems (CLT). The dependence of these estimators on the time lag carries information about H, and we exploit this to develop a rate-optimal estimator of roughness with a feasible CLT, valid also in the semimartingale case. In an empirical application to S&P 500 intra-day transaction data over 2018-2025, the leverage-based estimates of H fall below 1/2 throughout most of the sample, and the semimartingale hypothesis is rejected for the majority of the period since mid-2020.

detail.abstract: The Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP) gives the federal government, for the first time, the opportunity to negotiate "Maximum Fair Prices" (MFPs) for prescription drugs with manufacturers. The first ten drugs entered the program in 2026, and subsequent cohorts of 15-20 drugs are scheduled to be added each year. Covered entities enrolled in the 340B drug discount program are now eligible to purchase drugs from manufacturers at the lesser of the MFP and 340B price. However, they face revenue losses from statutory changes to Medicare reimbursement rates as well as spillover effects on prices negotiated with other payers. This study uses calibration methods to predict the impacts of the MDPNP on covered entities' net revenues from the 340B program in both the short and long run. I account for the reduction in costs from MFP pricing, the direct reduction in revenue from the new Medicare payment rules, and the indirect reduction in revenue from renegotiated prices with other payers. I identify preferred parameter values and also conduct sensitivity analyses. Using the preferred calibration of parameters, I predict that the MDPNP will reduce covered entities' net revenue from the 340B program by $5.73 billion in 2027, rising to over $24 billion per year by 2036 as more drugs enter the program. The projected long-term reduction represents about one-third of all 340B net revenues. Lowering prescription drug prices is an important policy objective. However, the manner in which the MDPNP does so presents a threat to the 340B program that will become increasingly severe over time.

detail.abstract: Since the 19th century, we have seen long-run waves of innovation: first with the introduction of machinery, then with the railroad boom, the creation and diffusion of electricity, the automobile boom, the nuclear power wave, and the internet and digitization boom. AI, as a new innovation wave, is best understood, at least for now, as a rapidly developing cluster of technologies within the wider information revolution, such as numerical, algorithmic, and software innovations, rather than as driven by a single-purpose technology. The scale and wide range of buildup, as well as the possible perils arising from them, make the AI investment boom an urgent case for examining a question that is both technological and financial: How does such a major wave of innovation influence capital and innovation investments? Does it drive excessive borrowing and an asset valuation boom, thereby increasing the economy's and financial market's vulnerability, possibly triggering deterioration in credit conditions, declining investments and cash flows, and widening credit spreads and deteriorating refinancing conditions, with sudden disruptions and corrections? Those joint structural changes on the real and financial sides create new governance and adaptive policy challenges. Fixed rules or fixed behavioral features can be costly and ill-suited to economic dynamics that move from new inventions and innovations to rapid diffusion, then to severe balancesheet stress, deleveraging, and possibly financial crashes. We propose a model-guided understanding of the interaction of a Schumpeterian innovation wave with Minskyan financial fragility dynamics. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is a useful numerical method to explore the dynamics in this setting because it solves finite-horizon adaptive policy problems starting from the current state and helps implement governance rules by considering the interactions of the various aspects.

detail.abstract: Over the last decade, AI has emerged as an important part of the scientific discovery enterprise. Its impacts, though, are not limited only to scientific discoveries, but also extend to the entire scientific ecosystem. In this paper, I develop a heuristic description of the scientific landscape to identify three main types of activities that scientists perform in that landscape -- landscape description and sharing; landscape integration; and landscape expansion -- and discuss how AI alters those activities. Leveraging that framing, I analyze conditions under which AI capabilities might support or hinder the broader aim of science to generate understanding. The analysis underscores the pivotal need for academia and industry to cooperate toward a degree of alignment consistent with the aims of science. Too much and too fast of a divergence in alignment -- as current times might be exhibiting -- also support potential policy action to prevent misalignment explosion.

detail.abstract: Does artificial intelligence substitute or complement high-skill labor? We study financial robo-advisors and their impact on the labor market for human advisors. Using novel data on robo-advisors and advisor employment, we find that robo-advisors increase, rather than reduce, human advisor employment. To address endogenous adoption, we exploit cross-state regulatory entry costs interacted with a national financing shock affecting technology firms. States experiencing greater robo-advisor entry exhibit meaningful growth in advisor employment, particularly among firms serving retail investors. Investor-level evidence shows robo-advisor exposure increases subsequent engagement with human advisors, consistent with market expansion and complementarity between automation and professional financial services.

detail.abstract: This chapter makes three contributions to dividend policy research. detail.abstract: Introduction: Investment advisers increasingly report using artificial intelligence (AI), but little is known about what they disclose about it in fiduciary filings. The SEC brought its first AI-washing enforcement actions in 2024, so regulators and researchers need a reproducible measure of AI disclosure. We provide largesample evidence on AI disclosure in Form ADV Part 2A brochures and show how the estimate depends on measurement design. Methods: We drew a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered investment advisers from a population of 16,223 firms, crossing adviser type (private-fund vs. wealth/retail) with 2024 assets-under-management (AUM) quartile. A large language model (LLM) classified the 388 available brochures under a prespecified five-label typology: investment-process use, operational or client-service use, AI-related risk, explicit non-use, and named AI vendors. We treated the LLM as a measurement instrument and validated it three ways: same-family reproducibility, blinded cross-family recoding of 180 brochures, and human verification of 158 cases. Secondary analyses compared brochures with 283 matched firm websites and applied a screen derived from SEC enforcement orders. Results: AI use is disclosed in 23.7% of brochures (22.7% survey-weighted), while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The within-brochure difference is significant (McNemar p = 0.036). Disclosure rises from 10.4% in the smallest AUM quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and is higher among private-fund advisers. Against human coding, the composite any-use measure achieves precision of 0.76 and sensitivity of 0.81. The same corpus yields estimates of 9.9%, 13.1%, and 23.7% under alternative constructs, adviser universes, and weighting schemes. A literal keyword rule misses or mislabels roughly a quarter of cases. A raw 17.3-percentage-point brochure-website gap disappears after conditioning on document length. None of the five enforcement-screen matches was adjudicated as an unsubstantiated promotional claim. Discussion: Advisers present AI at least as often as a risk as a capability, and disclosure is concentrated among larger and private-fund advisers. AI-disclosure prevalence reflects measurement design as much as adviser behavior, so estimates should be reported with their construct, universe, weighting, and validation. The validated framework and an open reproducibility capsule provide a baseline for monitoring AI claims and AI-washing in investment management.

detail.abstract:
This article analyzes one aspect of the dramatic shift in multilateral,
regional, and U.S. trade law from free trade, or at least managed trade, to
Aggressive Neo-Mercantilism. The article argues this economic shift enjoys
bipartisan support: through export control regulations during the Biden
interregnum (2021–2025) and the first 100 days (January 20-April 20, 2025)
of the Second Trump Administration, the U.S. seeks global production and
export dominance in advanced artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors.
America’s strategic goal, shared across the political aisle, is to impede the
People’s Republic of China (PRC) in its aspirations to develop sophisticated
chips. Simply put, restrictions (actual or proposed) on the cross-border flows
of advanced AI chips to a small number of preferred countries illustrate
industrial policy through export controls, which in turn is a hallmark of
America’s Aggressive Neo-Mercantilism.
To be sure, through its multiple new tariff regimes and threats
thereof, the second Trump Administration has been yet more aggressive than
its predecessor in attacking the multilateral trading system and free trade
agreements (FTAs). Its endgame for its attacks on the GATT-WTO and
NAFTA regimes seems to be xenophobic autarky—and that outcome does
not enjoy bipartisan support. But what is common across Administrations,
regardless of their political party, is a concern about the diffusion of national
security-related technologies to adversaries. That concern, though not
necessarily the specific export control regulations that manifest it, is as it
should be.

detail.abstract: Convertible bonds are three-to-five-year claims on equity volatility, yet the issuer often has no liquid long-dated options and only a short, noisy history. A one-parameter rule of thumb , maps an observed short-term volatility σ h into a long-term estimate σ i : it pulls very high observations down, pushes very low ones up and leaves the middle roughly alone. We test the rule out of sample on 99 listed stocks spanning eleven sectors and three size buckets, with histories of 20 to 52 years. Using a one-year volatility forecast as the input and the volatility realised over the following four years as the outcome, the median-fitted parameter is a = 0.61 (90% interval 0.55-0.65). This is stable across inputs and across threeto five-year horizons, and sits close to the practitioner prior a ≈ 0.7. The data are, if anything, more mean-reverting at the top of the range than the rule. We argue the shape follows from mean reversion in log volatility, and caution that the panel's survivorship biases the estimate toward too much reversion for high-volatility, weak-credit issuers-precisely the convertible universe. AI disclosure: an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) was used to run the experiments, write the code and draft the text; the idea and the rule are the author's own. * The views expressed are the author's own and do not necessarily represent those of Alken Asset Management.

detail.abstract: Since 2020, public spending on private school choice programs has doubled to $10 billion. In this paper, I document which students self-select into Indiana's private school voucher program and estimate the effect of voucher student exit on their classmates who are left behind in public schools. I find no evidence of positive selection into the voucher program. Instead, students with higher rates of past disciplinary infractions opt into the program. When students with disciplinary records exit, they cause 2.7 fewer in-school suspensions and 1.7 fewer out-of-school suspensions per 100 left-behind classmates. In contrast, the exit of students who do not have past disciplinary infractions causes no change in their left-behind classmates. My results suggest student reallocation improves the peer quality of public schools.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a genealogy of value for algorithmic capitalism. Its starting point is a problem that becomes increasingly visible when artificial intelligence, platforms, data infrastructures, and automated organizational systems are treated as autonomous sources of productivity: the economic result can remain measurable while the social and material conditions from which it derives become progressively harder to reconstruct. I call this process genealogical compression. It does not imply that labor disappears, nor that data replace labor as a new substance of value. Rather, heterogeneous contributions-past labor, organizational memory, public infrastructures, collective knowledge, classification practices, environmental resources, user activity, and institutional arrangements-are incorporated into technical systems and subsequently represented as properties of the asset, model, platform, or firm that controls them. Grounded in the Marxian problem of capitalist appropriation, the paper extends the distinction between incorporated labor and expelled labor into an inquiry into value derivability. This does not identify every socially useful contribution with surplus-valueproducing labor: surplus value, rent, competitive advantage, and transfers of value remain distinct mechanisms requiring distinct evidence. Derivability asks whether an attributed economic value can still be traced, with sufficient intelligibility, to the distributed conditions that made it possible. A system may therefore exhibit high accounting visibility and low genealogical visibility: profits, valuations, intellectualproperty claims, and productivity gains are observable, while the chain of contributions that sustains them is compressed or displaced. Artificial intelligence is treated not as the origin of this transformation but as a limiting case that makes an older capitalist tendency unusually legible. The argument has three consequences. First, data should be understood as historically produced and institutionally selected objects rather than pre-social raw material. Second, automation changes not only the quantity and organization of labor but also the attribution of authorship, productivity, and ownership. Third, distribution cannot be considered only after value has been produced, because rules of attribution already distribute recognition and entitlement at the moment value is constituted. The paper concludes by proposing genealogical compression and value derivability as critical instruments for investigating how socially produced capacities come under concentrated technical and economic control. Four situated trajectories-hotel work, supermarket operations, AI data work, and public infrastructures-clarify what must be investigated; they are not presented as four independently verified causal case studies. Reconstructing a contribution does not, by itself, prove surplus-value extraction, illegality, or a particular entitlement.

detail.abstract: Large manufacturers seeking to reduce corporate social responsibility (CSR) risks may gain access to suppliers with stronger compliance records. Such access appears to offer two benefits: improving supply chain compliance and diversifying random yield risk. However, reallocating orders can weaken the existing supplier's incentive to comply. To examine how introducing a responsible supplier affects supply chain compliance, we develop a game-theoretic model of a buyer and two potential suppliers with correlated random yields. The higher-cost responsible supplier always complies, whereas the lower-cost non-responsible supplier strategically decides whether to comply. The latter's compliance costs extend beyond the buyer's orders to its business with other customers. We first show that order commitments can substitute for auditing when the non-responsible supplier's outside business is of intermediate size. Second, we find that gaining access to the responsible supplier can paradoxically reduce the supply chain's CSR performance, measured by the compliant share of procurement, when the audit cost is below the relevant threshold and the non-responsible supplier's outside business is of intermediate size: diverting orders from the lower-cost supplier weakens its compliance incentive, and the resulting decline in compliance can outweigh the direct benefit of sourcing from the responsible supplier. To reconcile risk diversification with improved compliance, we examine peerto-peer training as a potential solution. By sharing compliance expertise, the responsible supplier can reduce the non-responsible supplier's compliance costs. We establish sufficient conditions under which such training benefits the buyer and both suppliers while increasing the supply chain's CSR performance. Our findings inform manufacturers' CSR management by clarifying how order allocation, auditing, and peer-to-peer supplier training can jointly shape supply chain compliance.

detail.abstract: Do the return anomalies documented in developed markets exist on the Moscow Exchange once the number of tests is taken into account? Under a protocol fixed before estimation, I test implementations of 25 price-, trading-and payout-based predictors on MOEX shares (holding months 2012:01-2026:09; share data free of survivorship bias, depositary receipts covered only in part) against a ladder of seven significance criteria. Seven characteristics clear |t| > 1.96 in the predicted direction. At the nominal 5% level the Romano-Wolf stepdown with a stationary bootstrap retains five: four closely related measures of intermediate-horizon momentum-nearness to the 52-week high, six-and twelvemonth and residual momentum-and a high-volume premium. Because the bootstrap test is mildly liberal at this sample length, I also calibrate its level by simulation; at the calibrated level of 0.03 only the four momentum signals remain. The high-volume premium is fragile: it fails the calibrated level, several robustness variants and trading costs. Correcting the 2013 trading data of 22 shares leaves these results unchanged. The four momentum signals are largely redundant rather than four independent discoveries. In this sample the bootstrap critical value (3.39) exceeds both the Harvey-Liu-Zhu hurdle and the normal-theory Bonferroni bound. The implemented low-risk, size, liquidity-level, skewness, seasonality and dividend-yield signals do not survive, but premia with annual Sharpe ratios below about one would often go undetected in a sample of this length. Among liquid shares last month's winners keep winning. Momentum remains significant net of estimated spread costs, but its capacity in equal-weighted form is small. After the 2022 exclusion of foreign investors no premium changes significantly once the tests are corrected for multiplicity, but the confidence intervals are wide.

detail.abstract: Industry 4.0 connects industrial assets, sensors, automation platforms, and data services, creating opportunities to identify degradation before it develops into costly failure. Yet the practical value of predictive maintenance depends not simply on deploying machine-learning models, but on connecting reliable condition data to trustworthy anomaly detection, diagnosis, remaining useful life estimation, and maintenance decisions. This review synthesizes established research on intelligent condition monitoring with emphasis on deep learning, industrial anomaly detection, edge-cloud architectures, and implementation constraints. It distinguishes condition monitoring, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, and prognostics as related but non-interchangeable tasks. Conventional signal-processing and machine-learning approaches remain useful where data are limited and interpretability is important; deep neural networks can learn complex representations from vibration, acoustic, electrical, thermal, process, and visual data, but their performance may deteriorate under operatingcondition changes, class imbalance, sensor faults, and distribution shift. Recent reviews emphasize the growing role of integrated architectures, digital twins, industrial Internet of Things infrastructure, and human-centred maintenance workflows (Gupta et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Zafar et al., 2024). A conceptual five-layer framework is proposed, linking sensing, data engineering, analytics, decision support, and action-oriented feedback. The framework highlights uncertainty communication, cybersecurity, interoperability, and maintenance-worker oversight as cross-cutting requirements. The paper concludes that progress should be evaluated through prospective industrial validation, calibrated risk measures, decision utility, and lifecycle cost-not predictive accuracy alone. As a literature-based conceptual review, it reports no new experiments or original empirical results.
